examples.title: Relationships between Middle School Students' Digital Literacy Skills, Computer Programming Self-Efficacy, and Computational Thinking Self-Efficacy
examples.abstract: This study aims to explain the relationships between secondary school students' digital literacy, computer programming self-efficacy and computational thinking self-efficacy. The study group consists of 204 secondary school students. A relational survey model was used in the research method and three different data collection tools were used to collect data. The structural equation model was used in data analysis to reveal a model that explains and predicts the relationships between variables. According to the results of the research, it was determined that digital literacy of secondary school students affected their computer programming self-efficacy, digital literacy affected their computational thinking self-efficacy, and computer programming self-efficacy affected their computational thinking self-efficacy. It was also found that digital literacy skills have an indirect effect on secondary students' computational thinking self-efficacy on computational thinking self-efficacy.
examples.note: School-age future-skills study (middle-school / adolescent digital literacy, 21st-century skills); in scope.

examples.title: Urban Middle School Students, Twenty-First Century Skills, and STEM-ICT Careers: Selected Findings from a Front-End Analysis
examples.abstract: As part of the design and development of an informal learning environment meant to increase urban middle school students' interest in technology-focused STEM careers, and to support their twenty-first century skill development, researchers developed and administered the ICT/Twenty-First Century Skills Questionnaire. Both STEM-ICT professionals and middle school students completed the survey. STEM-ICT professionals indicated that problem solving, critical thinking and communication were the most valued and the most frequently used skills in their environments. Students underestimated the amount of critical thinking and systematic design, and overestimated the amount of coding and digital research that occurs in STEM-ICT workplaces. Among skills highly valued by ICT professionals, students reported significantly lower ability levels in problem solving, critical thinking, communication, use of technical systems and information literacy. The researchers discuss implications of this research on future curriculum and program design.
examples.note: School-age future-skills study (middle-school / adolescent digital literacy, 21st-century skills); in scope.

examples.title: Adolescents' Perspectives about Their Digital and Connective Literacies
examples.abstract: As a term, "connective literacies" refers to the reading, writing, speaking, listening, viewing, and critical thinking skills necessary for students to engage and interact meaningfully, productively, and safely in a variety of digitally connected spaces. Using a critical literacies approach to honor the voices of adolescents as producers and consumers of online texts, in the present study, researchers conducted two focus groups of nine eighth-grade students. Adolescents shared their insights about their use of connective literacy skills in and outside of school, including how they use digital technologies, and how they connect with others in digital spaces. Researchers share and discuss five thematic findings, using transcript excerpts as illustrations to present adolescents' perspectives. Finally, we offer future directions for educators, policymakers, researchers, families, and students to advance adolescents' connective literacy skills.
examples.note: School-age future-skills study (middle-school / adolescent digital literacy, 21st-century skills); in scope.

examples.title: Teachers' Adoption of Generative AI Tools for Lesson Planning and Grading Workload
examples.abstract: This survey study examines how in-service teachers adopt generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT to reduce their lesson-planning and grading workload. Using a technology acceptance model, we surveyed 312 teachers about perceived usefulness, ease of use, and time saved when delegating administrative and preparation tasks to AI assistants. Findings indicate that perceived workload reduction is the strongest predictor of sustained tool use, while concerns about output accuracy moderate adoption. The study offers recommendations for schools seeking to support teachers' professional use of AI productivity tools.
examples.note: Hard FP class (teacher tool-use): the studied outcome is teachers' own productivity/adoption of AI tools, not a future skill cultivated in 6-18 learners. Matches 'generative ai' + 'teacher' so the heuristic keeps it.

examples.title: How Secondary School Teachers Use ChatGPT to Automate Administrative Communication
examples.abstract: Drawing on interviews with twenty secondary school teachers, this paper explores how educators integrate ChatGPT into routine administrative communication, including parent emails, report comments, and meeting minutes. We analyze the workflows teachers build around the tool and the time savings they report. The contribution is a typology of teacher-facing AI automation practices; student learning outcomes are out of scope for this study, which centers on teacher labor and administrative efficiency.
examples.note: Hard FP class (teacher tool-use): teacher administrative workflow, not a learner future-skill outcome. 'chatgpt' + 'secondary school'/'teacher' keep it through the heuristic.

examples.title: Teachers' Use of AI Chatbot Tools for Generating Classroom Quiz Questions
examples.abstract: This design study reports on a six-week deployment in which teachers used an AI chatbot to generate quiz questions and rubric drafts. We measured teacher satisfaction, editing effort, and perceived quality of the machine-generated items. The focus is on the teacher as the user of the artificial intelligence tool and on the practicality of AI authoring assistants for instructional preparation, rather than on any change in pupils' competencies.
examples.note: Hard FP class (teacher tool-use): teacher-as-tool-user, no measured 6-18 learner skill. 'artificial intelligence' + 'teacher'/'classroom' keep it.

examples.title: Disaster Risk Reduction and Hygiene Education: Building Resilience among Primary School Children
examples.abstract: This intervention study evaluates a disaster risk reduction and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) programme delivered in primary schools. Outcomes include children's handwashing behaviour, latrine use, and preparedness for floods and earthquakes. While the programme is framed around community resilience, its measured endpoints are public-health and physical-safety behaviours rather than cognitive or socio-emotional competencies.
examples.note: Hard FP class (disaster/health with a school word): a WASH/disaster-safety study whose real domain is public health. The off-scope term 'hygiene'/'sanitation' is exempted because 'resilience' appears in the title with a school-age audience, so the heuristic keeps it.

examples.title: Earthquake Preparedness and Critical Thinking among Secondary School Students
examples.abstract: This study assesses an earthquake preparedness curriculum for secondary school students and its association with disease prevention and post-disaster sanitation knowledge. Although the title frames the work around critical thinking about hazards, the instrument measures factual disaster-safety and public-health knowledge rather than transferable reasoning skills. The contribution is to disaster education and adolescent health behaviour.
examples.note: Hard FP class (disaster/health with a school word): disaster-safety and health knowledge, not a cultivated future skill. The off-scope 'disease'/'sanitation' terms are exempted by 'critical thinking' in the title plus a school-age audience, so the heuristic keeps it.

examples.title: Nutrition, Hygiene and Self-Regulation: A School Health Promotion Program for Adolescents
examples.abstract: We report on a school health promotion program for adolescents combining nutrition education, menstrual hygiene management, and goal-setting routines described as self-regulation. The evaluated outcomes are dietary intake, hygiene practices, and body-mass index. The self-regulation framing is incidental scaffolding for the health behaviours; the study's domain is adolescent public health, not future-skills education.
examples.note: Hard FP class (disaster/health with a school word): a nutrition/hygiene school-health study. The off-scope 'nutrition'/'hygiene'/'menstrual' terms are exempted by 'self-regulation' in the title with a school-age audience, so the heuristic keeps it.

examples.abstract: In einer Feldstudie an Gymnasien wird untersucht, wie adaptive KI-Lernsysteme das selbstregulierte Lernen unterstützen. Metakognition und Lernstrategien verbessern sich in der Interventionsgruppe.
